blog_summary: Adrian Colyer highlights SLOG as a system designed to provide strict serializability with low latency for geo-replicated transactions, addressing the challenge of coordination overhead in distributed systems. The key insight is leveraging region affinity—where data is likely accessed in its home region—to minimize cross-region coordination. SLOG achieves high throughput by processing most transactions within a single region using deterministic planning (similar to Calvin), while handling multi-home transactions with additional coordination. The paper introduces two models: SLOG-B (no cross-region sync) and SLOG-HA (sync to nearby regions), and evaluates SLOG against Calvin, NuoDB, and Cloud Spanner, showing superior latency for single-home transactions despite slight throughput disadvantages in multi-home scenarios.
paper_abstract: For decades, applications deployed on a world-wide scale have been forced to give up at least one of (1) strict serializability (2) low latency writes (3) high transactional throughput. In this paper we discuss SLOG: a system that avoids this tradeoff for workloads which contain physical region locality in data access. SLOG achieves high-throughput, strictly serializable ACID transactions at geo-replicated distance and scale for all transactions submitted across the world, all the while achieving low latency for transactions that initiate from a location close to the home region for data they access. Experiments find that SLOG can reduce latency by more than an order of magnitude relative to state-of-the-art strictly serializable geo-replicated database systems such as Spanner and Calvin, while maintaining high throughput under contention. PVLDB Reference Format: Kun Ren, Dennis Li, and Daniel J. Abadi. SLOG: Serializable, Low-latency, Geo-replicated Transactions. PVLDB, 12(11): 1747-1761, 2019. DOI: https://doi.org/10.14778/3342263.3342647
